title: Perfect Squares and Their Roots: Squaring and Rooting Undo Each Other
preview: Square a number, then root it — you're back where you started. A slice that builds squaring and square-rooting as inverses, then tests whether roots split across + and ×.

body.goal: Build squaring and taking the square root of a perfect square as inverse operations, and discover that a root distributes over multiplication and division but NOT over addition and subtraction.
body.launch: These all use PERFECT squares, so every answer is a whole number. Reveal one at a time. When two steps look alike but give different answers, stop and ask the class why.
body.prerequisiteLabel: Warm up the perfect squares before we take roots.

steps.teacherNote: The root undoes the square — back to 6.
Square THEN root returns the original number.
Root THEN square also returns the original. The two operations are inverses.
√25 = 5. Compare to the previous step: 7 ≠ 5, so √a + √b is NOT √(a+b).
√100 = 10. This MATCHES the previous step: √a × √b DOES equal √(ab).
7 − 2. (And √(49 − 4) = √45 is not even a whole number — subtraction doesn't split cleanly either.)

enrichmentSteps.problem: Is √(36 + 64) equal to √36 + √64? Show why or why not.
enrichmentSteps.answer: No. √(36+64) = √100 = 10, but √36 + √64 = 6 + 8 = 14. Roots do not split over addition.

body.consolidation: Two big ideas: (1) squaring and square-rooting a perfect square undo each other — √(n²) = n and (√n)² = n. (2) A square root splits over multiplication and division (√(ab) = √a·√b) but NOT over addition or subtraction. Have students state both rules in their own words and give a counterexample for the addition case.
